# Google Meet's New Homepage: What It Is and How to Get the Most Out of It

> **In short:** Google Meet has been quietly reshaping its homepage into a single hub where meeting agendas, attachments, notes, recordings, and transcripts live together. Below is what the new layout actually does, the Google Meet features you can pair it with today, and a few honest caveats about availability.

You've just finished a 45-minute call. Someone mentioned a decision that affects your whole team. Now you're scrolling back through your inbox, your Drive folders, three different chat threads — trying to find the notes, the recording, the attachment from the agenda. Sound familiar?

Google Meet's redesigned homepage is meant to turn that scavenger hunt into a single page you can scroll. Here's what it actually does, and how to use it without getting lost in the rollout.

## What the homepage now pulls together

Think of the old Meet experience like walking into a meeting room and being handed a single sheet of paper with the agenda on it — everything else (notes, recording, follow-ups) lived somewhere else. The new homepage is closer to a project folder for each meeting: one spot to see what the call was about, what was shared, and what came out of it.

In plain terms, Google says the homepage now surfaces:

- **Meeting details and attachments** from the linked Google Calendar invite
- **Notes, recordings, and transcripts** from past meetings, once the meeting is over
- A clear list of **upcoming meetings** so you can prep before walking in

If you've ever lost a recording or spent ten minutes hunting for the PDF someone shared right before the call, this is the part you'll appreciate most.

## Three real Google Meet features to pair with the homepage

Even if your account hasn't fully rolled out the new layout yet, the building blocks below are real and available today.

### 1. Link Meet to a Google Calendar invite

Every scheduled Meet call is created from a Calendar event. Open the event, and you'll see the Meet link, the agenda, and any attachments the organizer added. Treat that Calendar event as the "home page" for the meeting — it's where everything is supposed to anchor.

### 2. Turn on "Take notes for me"

This is Google's built-in AI note-taker. During a meeting, it listens to the call and writes a summary, which gets attached to the event. To use it, click the **Activities** menu (the three dots or the sparkle icon, depending on your version) inside the Meet call, then choose **Take notes for me**. The notes appear in the linked Calendar event when the meeting ends.

### 3. Record the meeting (organizers only)

If you're the meeting organizer or have been given recording access, click the **three-dot menu** in the call and pick **Record meeting**. The recording and transcript land in the organizer's **Meet Recordings** folder in Google Drive, and the transcript is also attached to the Calendar event.

> Quick note: "Take notes for me" and recording both require the meeting to be on a Workspace account with those features turned on — they're not available on every personal Google account.

## A few ways to actually use it day-to-day

- **Before a meeting:** Spend 60 seconds skimming the agenda and attachments inside the Calendar event. You'll walk in more prepared.
- **During the meeting:** Switch on **Take notes for me** so you don't have to type while people talk.
- **After the meeting:** Open the Calendar event (or the new Meet homepage, once it's live for you). Recording, transcript, and notes should all be there.

## What this means for you

- **For everyday life:** If you use Meet for a community group, a study group, or a family catch-up, the redesigned homepage means less "where's that link?" in the chat. Attach a PDF, record the call, and everyone can revisit it later without you forwarding files.
- **For work or business:** Treat the homepage as your meeting archive. At the end of each week, glance back through the week's calls. You'll spot decisions you forgot about and follow-ups that slipped.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one regular meeting and run the full cycle — attach an agenda to the Calendar event, switch on notes during the call, then check the homepage after. After a week, you'll see why it matters.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Waiting for the new layout before you start organizing.** The Calendar-event + "Take notes for me" + recording workflow is available today, even before the new homepage finishes rolling out.
- **Forgetting to actually click "Take notes for me."** The feature is off by default. If you don't turn it on, no notes appear later.
- **Looking for the recording in the wrong place.** Recordings go to the organizer's Google Drive, under **My Drive → Meet Recordings**. They don't email themselves to attendees.
- **Sharing the recording link without checking permissions.** Drive links can be too open. Restrict to "anyone with the link" or specific people before you paste it into a chat.

## The honest part

Google rolls features out gradually across accounts. If you don't see the redesigned homepage yet, that's normal — it's still reaching everyone. The Calendar event, the **Take notes for me** toggle, and the **Record meeting** option in the three-dot menu are the three building blocks worth learning today, because they work regardless of which version of the homepage your account shows.

## Wrap-up

The new Google Meet homepage is a small layout change that quietly solves a big everyday frustration: where do my meeting things actually live? By tying agendas, notes, and recordings to the Calendar event — and pulling them into one hub — it turns each meeting from a scattered pile of files into a tidy, searchable record. Open meet.google.com, glance at what's coming up, and let the page do the remembering for you.
